claim: Under current neurocomputational theories, preference reversals are typically interpreted in terms of errors that arise from the unreliable signaling of value to brain decision systems.
source: Under current neurocomputational theories, such preference reversals are typically interpreted in terms of errors that arise from the unreliable signaling of value to brain decision systems.
evidence: This is a statement about existing theories in the field, referencing established interpretations in neurocomputational literature.

claim: People may change their mind because they are reassessing the value of alternative options while pondering the decision.
source: But, an alternative explanation is that people may change their mind because they are reassessing the value of alternative options while pondering the decision.
evidence: This is the authors' proposed alternative explanation, presented as a theoretical possibility.

claim: Fast and automatic processes first provide initial (and largely uncertain) representations of options' values, yielding prior estimates of decision difficulty.
source: In brief, we assume that fast and automatic processes first provide initial (and largely uncertain) representations of options' values, yielding prior estimates of decision difficulty.
evidence: This is a core assumption of the MCD model presented by the authors.

claim: The allocation of cognitive resources is controlled by an effort-confidence tradeoff.
source: These uncertain value representations are then refined by deploying cognitive (e.g., attentional, mnesic) resources, the allocation of which is controlled by an effort-confidence tradeoff.
evidence: This is a fundamental assumption of the MCD model.

claim: The anticipated benefit of allocating resources varies in a decision-by-decision manner according to the prior estimate of decision difficulty.
source: Importantly, the anticipated benefit of allocating resources varies in a decision-by-decision manner according to the prior estimate of decision difficulty.
evidence: This is a prediction derived from the MCD model framework.

claim: The MCD model predicts response time, subjective feeling of effort, choice confidence, changes of mind, as well as choice-induced preference change and certainty gain.
source: The ensuing MCD model predicts response time, subjective feeling of effort, choice confidence, changes of mind, as well as choice-induced preference change and certainty gain.
evidence: This is a statement of the model's predictive scope.

claim: Snap judgments about others are prone to unconscious stereotyping, which often has enduring and detrimental consequences.
source: For example, snap judgments about others are prone to unconscious stereotyping, which often has enduring and detrimental consequences (Greenwald and Banaji, 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Biased and/or inaccurate decisions can be triggered by stress.
source: Biased and/or inaccurate decisions can be triggered by psychobiological determinants such as stress (Porcelli and Delgado, 2009; Porcelli et al., 2012), emotions (Harlé and Sanfey, 2007; De Martino et al., 2006; Sokol-Hessner et al., 2013), or fatigue (Blain et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to empirical studies.

claim: Biased and/or inaccurate decisions can be triggered by emotions.
source: Biased and/or inaccurate decisions can be triggered by psychobiological determinants such as stress (Porcelli and Delgado, 2009; Porcelli et al., 2012), emotions (Harlé and Sanfey, 2007; De Martino et al., 2006; Sokol-Hessner et al., 2013), or fatigue (Blain et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to empirical studies.

claim: Biased and/or inaccurate decisions can be triggered by fatigue.
source: Biased and/or inaccurate decisions can be triggered by psychobiological determinants such as stress (Porcelli and Delgado, 2009; Porcelli et al., 2012), emotions (Harlé and Sanfey, 2007; De Martino et al., 2006; Sokol-Hessner et al., 2013), or fatigue (Blain et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to empirical research.

claim: Biased and inaccurate decisions arise in the absence of contextual factors such as stress, emotions, or fatigue.
source: But, in fact, they also arise in the absence of such contextual factors.
evidence: This is presented as an established observation in the field.

claim: Decision errors are sometimes viewed as the outcome of inherent neurocognitive limitations on the brain's decision processes.
source: That is why they are sometimes viewed as the outcome of inherent neurocognitive limitations on the brain's decision processes, e.g., bounded attentional and/or mnemonic capacity (Giguère and Love, 2013; Lim et al., 2011; Marois and Ivanoff, 2005), unreliable neural representations of decision-relevant information (Drugowitsch et al., 2016; Wang and Busemeyer, 2016; Wyart and Koechlin, 2016), or physiologically constrained neural information transmission (Louie and Glimcher, 2012; Polanía et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to theoretical and empirical work.

claim: The brain has a preference for efficiency over accuracy.
source: However, an alternative perspective is that the brain has a preference for efficiency over accuracy (Thorngate, 1980).
evidence: This is presented as an alternative theoretical perspective with citation support.

claim: When making perceptual or motor decisions, people frequently trade accuracy for speed, even when time constraints are not tight.
source: For example, when making perceptual or motor decisions, people frequently trade accuracy for speed, even when time constraints are not tight (Heitz, 2014; Palmer et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: Neural and behavioral data are best explained by 'accumulation-to-bound' process models, in which a decision is emitted when the accumulated perceptual evidence reaches a bound.
source: Related neural and behavioral data are best explained by 'accumulation-to-bound' process models, in which a decision is emitted when the accumulated perceptual evidence reaches a bound (Gold and Shadlen, 2007; O'Connell et al., 2012; Ratcliff and McKoon, 2008; Ratcliff et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to empirical and theoretical work.

claim: If the bound is properly set, accumulation-to-bound models implement an optimal solution to speed-accuracy tradeoff problems.
source: Further computational work demonstrated that if the bound is properly set, these models actually implement an optimal solution to speed-accuracy tradeoff problems (Ditterich, 2006; Drugowitsch et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to computational studies.

claim: Accumulation-to-bound policies can be viewed as an evolutionary adaptation, in response to selective pressure that favors efficiency.
source: From a theoretical standpoint, this implies that accumulation-to-bound policies can be viewed as an evolutionary adaptation, in response to selective pressure that favors efficiency (Pirrone et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference from computational work, supported by citation.

claim: In contrast to evidence-based decisions, there are no right or wrong value-based decisions.
source: This is because, in contrast to evidence-based (e.g., perceptual) decisions, there are no right or wrong value-based decisions.
evidence: This is presented as a fundamental distinction in decision-making research.

claim: People make choices that deviate from subjective reports of value, with a rate that decreases with value contrast.
source: Nevertheless, people still make choices that deviate from subjective reports of value, with a rate that decreases with value contrast.
evidence: This is presented as an empirical observation in the field.

claim: From the perspective of accumulation-to-bound models, preference reversals count as errors and arise from the unreliable signaling of value to decision systems in the brain.
source: From the perspective of accumulation-to-bound models, these preference reversals count as errors and arise from the unreliable signaling of value to decision systems in the brain (Lim et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a statement about how accumulation-to-bound models interpret preference reversals, supported by citation.

claim: Value-based variants of accumulation-to-bound models are able to capture the neural and behavioral effects of overt attention.
source: That value-based variants of accumulation-to-bound models are able to capture the neural and behavioral effects of, e.g., overt attention (Krajbich et al., 2010; Lim et al., 2011), external time pressure (Milosavljevic et al., 2010), confidence (De Martino et al., 2013), or default preferences (Lopez-Persem et al., 2016) lends empirical support to this type of interpretation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: Value-based variants of accumulation-to-bound models are able to capture the neural and behavioral effects of external time pressure.
source: That value-based variants of accumulation-to-bound models are able to capture the neural and behavioral effects of, e.g., overt attention (Krajbich et al., 2010; Lim et al., 2011), external time pressure (Milosavljevic et al., 2010), confidence (De Martino et al., 2013), or default preferences (Lopez-Persem et al., 2016) lends empirical support to this type of interpretation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to empirical research.

claim: Value-based variants of accumulation-to-bound models are able to capture the neural and behavioral effects of confidence.
source: That value-based variants of accumulation-to-bound models are able to capture the neural and behavioral effects of, e.g., overt attention (Krajbich et al., 2010; Lim et al., 2011), external time pressure (Milosavljevic et al., 2010), confidence (De Martino et al., 2013), or default preferences (Lopez-Persem et al., 2016) lends empirical support to this type of interpretation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to empirical research.

claim: Value-based variants of accumulation-to-bound models are able to capture the neural and behavioral effects of default preferences.
source: That value-based variants of accumulation-to-bound models are able to capture the neural and behavioral effects of, e.g., overt attention (Krajbich et al., 2010; Lim et al., 2011), external time pressure (Milosavljevic et al., 2010), confidence (De Martino et al., 2013), or default preferences (Lopez-Persem et al., 2016) lends empirical support to this type of interpretation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to empirical research.

claim: Under some simplifying assumptions, accumulation-to-bound process models optimally solve the problem of efficient value comparison.
source: Further credit also comes from theoretical studies showing that these process models, under some simplifying assumptions, optimally solve the problem of efficient value comparison (Tajima et al., 2016; Tajima et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical studies.

claim: Accumulation-to-bound models do not solve the issue of adjusting the amount of effort to invest in reassessing an uncertain prior preference with yet-unprocessed value-relevant information.
source: However, they do not solve the issue of adjusting the amount of effort to invest in reassessing an uncertain prior preference with yet-unprocessed value-relevant information.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of the limitations of accumulation-to-bound models.

claim: Mental effort is optimally traded against choice confidence, given how value representations are modified while pondering decisions.
source: Here, we propose an alternative computational model of value-based decision-making that suggests that mental effort is optimally traded against choice confidence, given how value representations are modified while pondering decisions (Slovic, 1995; Tversky and Thaler, 1990; Warren et al., 2011).
evidence: This is the core proposal of the MCD model, with supporting citations.

claim: The brain generates representations of options' value in a quick and automatic manner, even before attention is engaged for comparing option values.
source: We start from the premise that the brain generates representations of options' value in a quick and automatic manner, even before attention is engaged for comparing option values (Lebreton et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a premise of the MCD model, supported by citation.

claim: The brain encodes the certainty of value estimates.
source: The brain also encodes the certainty of such value estimates (Lebreton et al., 2015), from which a priori feelings of choice difficulty and confidence could, in principle, be derived.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to empirical research.

claim: People are reluctant to make a choice that they are not confident about.
source: Importantly, people are reluctant to make a choice that they are not confident about (De Martino et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to empirical research.

claim: When faced with a difficult decision, people should reassess option values until they reach a satisfactory level of confidence about their preference.
source: Thus, when faced with a difficult decision, people should reassess option values until they reach a satisfactory level of confidence about their preference.
evidence: This is a prediction derived from the MCD model framework.

claim: Effortful mental deliberation engages neurocognitive resources, such as attention and memory, in order to process value-relevant information.
source: This effortful mental deliberation would engage neurocognitive resources, such as attention and memory, in order to process value-relevant information.
evidence: This is an assumption of the MCD model.

claim: The amount of allocated resources optimizes a tradeoff between expected effort cost and confidence gain.
source: In line with recent proposals regarding the strategic deployment of cognitive control (Musslick et al., 2015; Shenhav et al., 2013), we assume that the amount of allocated resources optimizes a tradeoff between expected effort cost and confidence gain.
evidence: This is an assumption of the MCD model, aligned with cited theoretical frameworks.

claim: The MCD model adjusts mental effort on a decision-by-decision basis, according to prior decision difficulty and importance.
source: The ensuing metacognitive control of decisions or MCD thus adjusts mental effort on a decision-by-decision basis, according to prior decision difficulty and importance (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a key feature of the MCD model, illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: A total of 41 people participated in this study.
source: A total of 41 people (28 female; age: mean = 28, SD = 5, min = 20, max = 40) participated in this study.
evidence: This is a direct report of the study's sample size.

claim: The experiment lasted approximately 2 hours.
source: The experiment lasted approximately 2 hr, and participants were paid a flat rate of 20€ as compensation for their time, plus a bonus, which was given to participants to compensate for potential financial losses in the 'penalized' trials (see below).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental procedure.

claim: In 'penalized' trials, participants lost 0.20€ for each second that they took to make their choice.
source: More precisely, in 'penalized' trials, participants lost 0.20€ (out of a 5€ bonus) for each second that they took to make their choice.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental procedure.

claim: The average bonus across participants was 4€.
source: This resulted in an average 4€ bonus (across participants).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental outcome data.

claim: The stimuli for this experiment were 148 digital images, each representing a distinct food item.
source: The stimuli for this experiment were 148 digital images, each representing a distinct food item (50 fruits, 50 vegetables, and 48 various snack items including nuts, meats, and cheeses).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental materials.

claim: Eye gaze position and pupil size were continuously recorded throughout the duration of the experiment using The Eye Tribe eye-tracking devices.
source: Eye gaze position and pupil size were continuously recorded throughout the duration of the experiment using The Eye Tribe eye-tracking devices.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental procedure.

claim: The choice section of the experiment was composed of 60 'neutral' trials, 7 'consequential' trials, and 7 'penalized' trials.
source: The choice section of the experiment was composed of 60 'neutral' trials, 7 'consequential' trials, and 7 'penalized' trials, which were randomly intermixed.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental design.

claim: All across-trial correlations between observed and predicted (out-of-sample) data were statistically significant at the group-level (all p<10−3).
source: In fact, all across-trial correlations between observed and predicted (out-of-sample) data were statistically significant at the group-level (all p<10−3).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis results.

claim: The MCD model makes accurate out-of-sample predictions regarding effort-related variables given decision-related variables, and reciprocally.
source: In particular, this implies that the MCD model makes accurate out-of-sample predictions regarding effort-related variables given decision-related variables, and reciprocally.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the statistical analysis results.

claim: RT decreases when |ΔVR0| and/or VCR0 increases.
source: One can see that RT data behave as expected under the MCD model, that is, RT decreases when |ΔVR0|and/or VCR0 increases.
evidence: This is a summary of empirical findings from the study.

claim: |ΔVR0| has a significant negative effect on RT at the group level (mean standardized regression weight = −0.16, s.e.m. = 0.02, p<10−3).
source: The random effect analysis shows that both variables have a significant negative effect at the group level (|ΔVR0|: mean standardized regression weight = −0.16, s.e.m. = 0.02, p<10−3; VCR0: mean standardized regression weight = −0.08, s.e.m. = 0.02, p<10−3; one-sided t-tests).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis results.

claim: VCR0 has a significant negative effect on RT at the group level (mean standardized regression weight = −0.08, s.e.m. = 0.02, p<10−3).
source: The random effect analysis shows that both variables have a significant negative effect at the group level (|ΔVR0|: mean standardized regression weight = −0.16, s.e.m. = 0.02, p<10−3; VCR0: mean standardized regression weight = −0.08, s.e.m. = 0.02, p<10−3; one-sided t-tests).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis results.

claim: Subjective effort decreases when |ΔVR0| and/or VCR0 increases.
source: Here as well, subjective effort rating data behave as expected under the MCD model, that is, subjective effort decreases when |ΔVR0| and/or VCR0 increases.
evidence: This is a summary of empirical findings from the study.

claim: |ΔVR0| has a significant negative effect on subjective effort ratings at the group level (mean standardized regression weight = −0.21, s.e.m. = 0.03, p<10−3).
source: The random effect analysis shows that both variables have a significant negative effect at the group level (|ΔVR0|: mean standardized regression weight = −0.21, s.e.m. = 0.03, p<10−3; VCR0: mean regression weight = −0.05, s.e.m. = 0.02, p=0.027; one-sided t-tests).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis results.

claim: VCR0 has a significant negative effect on subjective effort ratings at the group level (mean regression weight = −0.05, s.e.m. = 0.02, p=0.027).
source: The random effect analysis shows that both variables have a significant negative effect at the group level (|ΔVR0|: mean standardized regression weight = −0.21, s.e.m. = 0.03, p<10−3; VCR0: mean regression weight = −0.05, s.e.m. = 0.02, p=0.027; one-sided t-tests).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis results.

claim: Both RT and subjective effort ratings were significantly higher for 'consequential' decisions than for 'neutral' decisions.
source: More precisely, both RT and subjective effort ratings were significantly higher for 'consequential' decisions than for 'neutral' decisions (log-RT: mean standardized regression weight = 0.07, s.e.m. = 0.03, p=0.036; effort ratings: mean standardized regression weight = 0.12, s.e.m. = 0.03, p<10−3; one-sided t-tests).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis results.

claim: Response times are significantly faster for 'penalized' than for 'neutral' decisions (mean standardized regression weight = −0.26, s.e.m. = 0.03, p<10−3).
source: In addition, response times are significantly faster for 'penalized' than for 'neutral' decisions (mean standardized regression weight = −0.26, s.e.m. = 0.03, p<10−3; one-sided t-test).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis results.

claim: The difference in subjective effort ratings between 'neutral' and 'penalized' decisions does not reach statistical significance (mean effort difference = 0.012, s.e.m. = 0.024, p=0.66).
source: However, the difference in subjective effort ratings between 'neutral' and 'penalized' decisions does not reach statistical significance (mean effort difference = 0.012, s.e.m. = 0.024, p=0.66; two-sided t-test).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis results.

claim: Under the MCD model, choice confidence reflects the discriminability of the options' value representations after optimal resource allocation.
source: Under the MCD model, choice confidence reflects the discriminability of the options' value representations after optimal resource allocation.
evidence: This is a theoretical statement about the MCD model.

claim: Both |ΔVR0| and VCR0 have a significant positive impact on choice confidence.
source: In brief, both |ΔVR0| (mean standardized regression weight = 0.25, s.e.m. = 0.02, p<10−3; one-sided t-test) and VCR0 (mean standardized regression weight = 0.16, s.e.m. = 0.03, p<10−3; one-sided t-test) have a significant positive impact on choice confidence.
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis results.

claim: On average, the rate of change of mind reaches about 14.5% (s.e.m. = 0.008, p<10−3).
source: Note that, on average, the rate of change of mind reaches about 14.5% (s.e.m. = 0.008, p<10−3, one-sided t-test), which is significantly higher than the rate of 'error' (mean rate difference = 2.3%, s.e.m. = 0.01, p=0.032; two-sided t-test).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis results.

claim: The rate of change of mind is significantly higher than the rate of 'error' (mean rate difference = 2.3%, s.e.m. = 0.01, p=0.032).
source: Note that, on average, the rate of change of mind reaches about 14.5% (s.e.m. = 0.008, p<10−3, one-sided t-test), which is significantly higher than the rate of 'error' (mean rate difference = 2.3%, s.e.m. = 0.01, p=0.032; two-sided t-test).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis results.

claim: Both |ΔVR0| and VCR0 have a significant negative impact on the rate of change of mind.
source: In brief, both |ΔVR0| (mean standardized regression weight = −0.17, s.e.m. = 0.02, p<10−3; one-sided t-test) and VCR0 (mean standardized regression weight = −0.08, s.e.m. = 0.03, p<10−3; one-sided t-test) have a significant negative impact on the rate of change of mind.
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis results.

claim: There is a significant positive spreading of alternatives (mean = 0.04 A.U., s.e.m. = 0.004, p<10−3).
source: One can see that there is a significant positive spreading of alternatives (mean = 0.04 A.U., s.e.m. = 0.004, p<10−3, one-sided t-test).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis results.

claim: Both |ΔVR0| and VCR0 have a significant negative impact on spreading of alternatives.
source: In addition, the results of the group-level random effect analysis confirm that both |ΔVR0| (mean standardized regression weight = −0.09, s.e.m. = 0.03, p=0.001; one-sided t-test) and VCR0 (mean standardized regression weight = −0.04, s.e.m. = 0.02, p=0.03; one-sided t-test) have a significant negative impact on spreading of alternatives.
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis results.

claim: The effect of |ΔVR0| and VCR0 on spreading of alternatives replicates previous findings on choice-induced preference change.
source: Note that this replicates previous findings on choice-induced preference change (Lee and Coricelli, 2020; Lee and Daunizeau, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work by the authors.

claim: There is a small but significantly positive certainty gain (mean = 0.11 A.U., s.e.m. = 0.06, p=0.027).
source: Importantly, there is a small but significantly positive certainty gain (mean = 0.11 A.U., s.e.m. = 0.06, p=0.027, one-sided t-test).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis results.

claim: VCR0 has a very strong negative impact on certainty gain (mean standardized regression weight = −0.61, s.e.m. = 0.04, p<10−3).
source: In brief, although VCR0 has a very strong negative impact on certainty gain (mean standardized regression weight = −0.61, s.e.m. = 0.04, p<10−3; one-sided t-test), the effect of |ΔVR0| does not reach statistical significance (mean standardized regression weight = −0.009, s.e.m. = 0.01, p=0.35; one-sided t-test).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis results.

claim: The effect of |ΔVR0| on certainty gain does not reach statistical significance (mean standardized regression weight = −0.009, s.e.m. = 0.01, p=0.35).
source: In brief, although VCR0 has a very strong negative impact on certainty gain (mean standardized regression weight = −0.61, s.e.m. = 0.04, p<10−3; one-sided t-test), the effect of |ΔVR0| does not reach statistical significance (mean standardized regression weight = −0.009, s.e.m. = 0.01, p=0.35; one-sided t-test).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis results.

claim: A simple regression-to-the-mean artifact likely inflates the observed negative correlation between VCR0 and certainty gain, beyond what would be predicted under the MCD model.
source: We note that a simple regression-to-the-mean artifact (Stigler, 1997) likely inflates the observed negative correlation between VCR0 and certainty gain, beyond what would be predicted under the MCD model.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results, with citation to the statistical concept.

claim: The MCD model provides an alternative theoretical framework to accumulation-to-bound models of decision-making.
source: As we will see, the MCD model makes clear quantitative predictions about several key decision variables (cf. Model section below). We test these predictions by asking participants to report their judgments about each item's subjective value and their subjective certainty about their value judgments, both before and after choosing between pairs of the items.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a key contribution of the work.

claim: Standard DDM variants make quantitative predictions regarding both response times and decision outcomes, but are agnostic about choice confidence, spreading of alternatives, value certainty gain, and/or subjective effort ratings.
source: Recall that DDMs assume that decisions are triggered once the noisy evidence in favor of a particular option has reached a predefined bound. Standard DDM variants make quantitative predictions regarding both response times and decision outcomes, but are agnostic about choice confidence, spreading of alternatives, value certainty gain, and/or subjective effort ratings.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of DDMs compared to the MCD model.

claim: Simple DDMs are significantly less accurate than MCD at making out-of-sample predictions on dependent variables common to both models.
source: We note that simple DDMs are significantly less accurate than MCD at making out-of-sample predictions on dependent variables common to both models (e.g., change of mind).
evidence: This is a comparative claim about model performance, with reference to additional analysis in the Appendix.

claim: The DDM provides an optimal solution to the problem of efficiently comparing option values, which may be unreliably signaled, but remain nonetheless stationary.
source: In contrast, the DDM provides an optimal solution to the problem of efficiently comparing option values, which may be unreliably signaled, but remain nonetheless stationary.
evidence: This is a characterization of what the DDM optimizes, contrasting it with the MCD model.

claim: The DDM cannot predict choice-induced preference changes, or changes in options' values more generally.
source: This is why the DDM cannot predict choice-induced preference changes, or changes in options' values more generally.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the limitations of DDMs.

claim: The MCD model assumes that the value representations themselves are modified during the decision process, in proportion to the effort expenditure.
source: In contrast, the MCD model assumes that the value representations themselves are modified during the decision process, in proportion to the effort expenditure.
evidence: This is a key distinguishing feature of the MCD model.

claim: The typical interpretation of spreading of alternatives is that of 'cognitive dissonance' reduction: if people feel uneasy about their choice, they later convince themselves that the chosen (rejected) item was actually better (worse) than they originally thought.
source: Its typical interpretation is that of 'cognitive dissonance' reduction: if people feel uneasy about their choice, they later convince themselves that the chosen (rejected) item was actually better (worse) than they originally thought (Bem, 1967; Harmon-Jones et al., 2009; Izuma and Murayama, 2013).
evidence: This is a statement about the traditional interpretation in the literature, supported by citations.

claim: Recent neuroimaging studies have shown that spreading of alternatives can be predicted from brain activity measured during the decision.
source: Interestingly, recent neuroimaging studies have shown that spreading of alternatives can be predicted from brain activity measured during the decision (Colosio et al., 2017; Jarcho et al., 2011; Kitayama et al., 2013; van Veen et al., 2009, Voigt et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to neuroimaging studies.

claim: Key regions of the brain's valuation and cognitive control systems are involved in spreading of alternatives, including: the right inferior frontal gyrus, the ventral striatum, the anterior insula, and the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC).
source: In addition, key regions of the brain's valuation and cognitive control systems are involved, including: the right inferior frontal gyrus, the ventral striatum, the anterior insula, and the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC).
evidence: This is a summary of neuroimaging findings from cited studies.

claim: The ACC is involved in controlling the allocation of cognitive effort.
source: This further corroborates the MCD interpretation, under the assumption that the ACC is involved in controlling the allocation of cognitive effort (Musslick et al., 2015; Shenhav et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Spreading of alternatives has a known statistical artifact component.
source: Having said this, both MCD and cognitive dissonance reduction mechanisms may contribute to spreading of alternatives, on top of its known statistical artifact component (Chen and Risen, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The statistical artifact component of spreading of alternatives is a consequence of the fact that pre-choice value ratings may be unreliable and is known to produce an apparent spreading of alternatives that decreases with pre-choice value difference.
source: The latter is a consequence of the fact that pre-choice value ratings may be unreliable and is known to produce an apparent spreading of alternatives that decreases with pre-choice value difference (Izuma and Murayama, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The effect of pre-choice value difference on spreading of alternatives is higher in the current study than in a control condition where the choice is made after both rating sessions.
source: Second, we have already shown that the effect of pre-choice value difference on spreading of alternatives is higher here than in a control condition where the choice is made after both rating sessions (Lee and Daunizeau, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Involving cognitive resources in value-related information processing is costly, which calls for an efficient resource allocation mechanism.
source: A central tenet of the MCD model is that involving cognitive resources in value-related information processing is costly, which calls for an efficient resource allocation mechanism.
evidence: This is a core assumption of the MCD model.

claim: Value-encoding neurons may have a bounded firing range.
source: A related notion is that information processing resources may be limited, in particular: value-encoding neurons may have a bounded firing range (Louie and Glimcher, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Efficient coding theory assumes that the brain has evolved adaptive neural codes that optimally account for capacity limitations.
source: In turn, 'efficient coding' theory assumes that the brain has evolved adaptive neural codes that optimally account for such capacity limitations (Barlow, 1961; Laughlin, 1981).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to foundational work in efficient coding theory.

claim: Efficient coding implies that value-encoding neurons should optimally adapt their firing range to the prior history of experienced values.
source: In our context, efficient coding implies that value-encoding neurons should optimally adapt their firing range to the prior history of experienced values (Polanía et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to recent research.

claim: When augmented with a Bayesian model of neural encoding/decoding, efficient coding was successful in explaining the non-trivial relationship between choice consistency and the distribution of subjective value ratings.
source: When augmented with a Bayesian model of neural encoding/decoding (Wei and Stocker, 2015), this idea was successful in explaining the non-trivial relationship between choice consistency and the distribution of subjective value ratings.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) was found to respond positively to both value difference and choice confidence.
source: First, the ventromedial prefrontal cortex or vmPFC was found to respond positively to both value difference (i.e., ΔVR0) and choice confidence.
evidence: This is a summary of neuroimaging findings from cited research (De Martino et al., 2013).

claim: The right rostrolateral prefrontal cortex (rRLPFC) was more active during low-confidence versus high-confidence choices.
source: Second, the right rostrolateral prefrontal cortex or rRLPFC was more active during low-confidence versus high-confidence choices.
evidence: This is a summary of neuroimaging findings from cited research (De Martino et al., 2013).

claim: Under the MCD framework, the contribution of the vmPFC to value-based decision control might be to construct item values, and to anticipate and monitor the benefit of effort investment (i.e., confidence).
source: Under the MCD framework, the contribution of the vmPFC to value-based decision control might rather be to construct item values, and to anticipate and monitor the benefit of effort investment (i.e., confidence).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of vmPFC function under the MCD framework.

claim: Recent fMRI studies suggest that vmPFC confidence computations signal the attainment of task goals.
source: This would be consistent with recent fMRI studies suggesting that vmPFC confidence computations signal the attainment of task goals (Hebscher and Gilboa, 2016; Lebreton et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to neuroimaging studies.

claim: The rRLPFC provides the neurocognitive resources that are instrumental for processing value-relevant information during decisions.
source: Thus, the puzzling negative correlation between choice confidence and rRLPFC activity could be simply explained under the assumption that rRLPFC provides the neurocognitive resources that are instrumental for processing value-relevant information during decisions (and/or to compare item values).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of rRLPFC function under the MCD framework.

claim: The rRLPFC is involved in reasoning.
source: This resonates with the known involvement of rRLPFC in reasoning (Desrochers et al., 2015; Dumontheil, 2014) or memory retrieval (Benoit et al., 2012; Westphal et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The rRLPFC is involved in memory retrieval.
source: This resonates with the known involvement of rRLPFC in reasoning (Desrochers et al., 2015; Dumontheil, 2014) or memory retrieval (Benoit et al., 2012; Westphal et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The MCD model can only explain 81% of the variability in dependent variables that can be captured using simple linear regressions against ΔVR0 and VCR0.
source: The fact that it can only explain 81% of the variability in dependent variables that can be captured using simple linear regressions against ΔVR0 and VCR0 (see section 11 of the Appendix) supports this notion.
evidence: This is a quantitative assessment of model performance, with reference to additional analysis.

claim: People spent more time and effort deciding between two disliked items than between two liked items, all else equal.
source: For example, we found that, all else equal, people spent more time and effort deciding between two disliked items than between two liked items (results not shown).
evidence: This is a report of an empirical finding from the study.

claim: The finding that people spend more time deciding between disliked items reproduces recent results regarding the evaluation of choice sets.
source: This reproduces recent results regarding the evaluation of choice sets (Shenhav and Karmarkar, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to recent research.

claim: A saturating type #2 efficacy brings no additional explanatory power for the model's dependent variables.
source: In brief, a saturating type #2 efficacy brings no additional explanatory power for the model's dependent variables.
evidence: This is a report of model comparison results, with reference to additional analysis in the Appendix.

claim: Rendering the cost term nonlinear (e.g., quadratic) does not change the qualitative nature of the MCD predictions.
source: Similarly, rendering the cost term nonlinear (e.g., quadratic) does not change the qualitative nature of the MCD predictions.
evidence: This is a statement about model robustness based on additional analyses.

claim: This study complies with all relevant ethical regulations and received formal approval from the INSERM Ethics Committee (CEEI-IRB00003888, decision no 16–333).
source: This study complies with all relevant ethical regulations and received formal approval from the INSERM Ethics Committee (CEEI-IRB00003888, decision no 16–333).
evidence: This is a direct statement about ethical compliance.

claim: All participants gave written informed consent prior to commencing the experiment.
source: In particular, in accordance with the Helsinki declaration, all participants gave written informed consent prior to commencing the experiment, which included consent to disseminate the results of the study via publication.
evidence: This is a direct statement about ethical procedures.
